author: PendragonY
title: My DGI Portfolio May Review
text:
What did I think at my last portfolio review? Last month I wrote about my DGI portfolio that I keep in an IRA account. Below is a chart from that article showing the dividends collected since 2015 by month. I have a goal of increasing dividends each year by 12% from the prior year's dividends, and since 2015 this DGI portfolio has met or exceeded that goal. While I was on track to meet my goal for 2018, my one concern was that the dividends collected in March of 2018 didn't exceed those collected in March of 2017. In large part that was due to one company CCP merging with a company and paying earlier and another company delaying its dividend payments to take advantage of the new tax laws treatment of dividends from REITS.
Figure 1 Portfolio Dividend Income as of May 3 2018
What happened during May? May being the last month before the start of summer, and bikini season, I made a number of moves in the portfolio to get it into shape for the summer. The table below is from my broker and lists the various trades. I have grouped them into 11 transactions which I will explain in more detail.
Transaction #1 is rolling the covered call I have on my 200 shares of Altria ( MO ). Because the price of MO has fallen a bit lately, I moved the expiration date out till June of 2019 and dropped the strike price to $65 from $70. I picked up a net credit of $239.10. I normally don't like to lower the strike price, but with MO trading around $55 it shouldn't be a problem. I'll likely roll this again, and if the price has moved up I can just roll the strike price up too.
I once just held 2 CEFs, ETO ( ETO ) and EXG( EXG ), but recently have added ETY ( ETY ) to the mix. So for transaction #2 I continued to move money from ETO to ETY. ETO and ETY are now about equal in size which is where I want them.
Transaction #3 is the first of 2 deployments of accumulated cash (primarily from dividends). I determined in this article that NextEra Energy ( NEE ) was the next utility I wanted to add to my portfolio. Looking at the results of the acquisition of a bunch of assets from Southern Corporation, I determined that NEE was even more attractive in this article . This is just the first purchase of NEE that I will be making over the rest of the year.
The SNF REIT sector has been seen a big decline in share prices. Part of that is because of increased risks. I had some $50K invested in REITS with significant exposure to SNFs. Transaction #4 was done to reduce my exposure to SNFs. Between LTC Properties ( LTC ), Omega Healthcare Investors ( OHI ) and Sabra Healthcare ( SBRA ), LTC is probably the safest but it also pays the smallest dividend. The monthly dividend has also not increased since June of 2016. So I decided to sell the LTC position. The LTC position produced $637.80 in yearly dividend income, so I wanted to purchase stocks that would replace that income. Dominion ( D ) pays $110.22, WP Carey ( WPC ) pays $247.66, Ladder Capital ( LADR ) pays $252 and EPR Properties ( EPR ) for a total of $648.76 projected dividend payments over the next 12 months. And each of those 4 are currently raising their dividends on an annual basis which LTC is not doing.
Transaction #5 was about shifting money from a monthly dividend paying REIT that hadn't raised its dividend since 2016 to a monthly payer that had raised its dividend regularly and last increased it at the beginning of the year. So I swapped 100 shares of Chatham Lodging ( CLDT ) out and got 32 more shares of EPR. The CLDT shares produced $132 in dividends a year while the replacement EPR shares produced $138.24. While the extra $6 of dividends a year is nice, the fact that EPR had bumped its dividend up 2 cents a month was a much more welcome increase.
Transaction #6 helps to further de-risk the OHI position by selling covered calls on the position. The first sale was for 3 contracts with a strike price of $30 and an expiration date of September of 2018. Sure enough the price trend in OHI then promptly reversed. So I closed out one of the contracts and rolled the other two out to an expiration date January of 2020 and a strike price of $32. I did all that for a net credit of approximately $72.
I was reading a comment by SA contributor Chowder when he mentioned that Cracker Barrel ( CBRL ) would be paying a special dividend in July. I ended up writing this article about CBRL and purchasing the stock as well. Transaction #7 was a swap of McDonald's ( MCD ) shares for CRBL. I also trimmed my position in Emerson Electric ( EMR ). As an industrial EMR is cyclical and sometimes I will trim it when it is at the high end of its cycle. Selling some EMR shares and all of my MCD shares allowed me to buy $120 CBRL shares. With EMR having a yield of 2.7% and MCD having a yield of 2.5%, the 3.2% yield of CBRL gives a nice boost to portfolio yield. But even better is the $3.75 special dividend to be paid on August 6th. If I don't add more shares of CBRL before July 13th, that will give me a $450 boost in August dividend payments.
Transaction #8 involved rolling the covered call I have on my Coke ( KO ) shares so that they now expire in November instead of August. That got me a net credit of around $57. The $45 strike price is around 20% more than I paid for the shares, and still around 5% OTM. There still are quite a few expiration dates later than the current contracts I have open, so if KO continues to increase in price I should have no problem rolling them out and up (meaning I push the expiration date later and the strike price higher).
On May 29th, I wrote an article about Kimco ( KIM ), a shopping center REIT. Because of how much of my portfolio is currently in REITS, I hadn't planned on buying KIM shares. However, one of the first comments posted to the article caused me to change my mind. I had a modest gain in Store Capital, so I sold just over 85 shares to bring my position down to 400 shares. I used that cash to buy 155 shares of KIM. The STOR shares would have paid around $106.28 in dividends while the new KIM shares will pay $173.60 over the next 12 months.
On May 29th I used accumulated cash (mostly from dividends) to buy $1500 worth of Apple ( AAPL ). I got just under 10 shares. I outlined why I was doing this and exactly how I found AAPL to be at a price I was willing to pay in this article . Going forward I will be alternating purchases of AAPL and NEE as long as each remain below my buy prices ($189 for AAPL and $171 for NEE). Since I next plan to buy some more NEE, AAPL has some time to drop back down into my buy range. Ordinarily I would let a stock I want go just because it was a dollar or so above my buy price, but I set the price for AAPL much higher than I would ordinarily because it is Apple.
The final transaction, #11, was done to both reduce how much I have in Stag Industrial ( STAG ) but also to increase my position in MAIN in time to capture the regular special dividend for June of $0.275 a share. With the new MAIN shares that will be $141.30. MAIN's 70 basis points higher yield doesn't hurt either.
Below is what my DGI portfolio in my IRA account looked like as of market close on Friday June 1.
Figure 2 DGI Portfolio positions as of close of Market June 1 2018
Figure 3 DGI Portfolio Dividend Income
In May I received $2711.73 in dividend payments, 47.85% higher than May of last year. For the year so far I have received $10,760.39, 23.19% higher than at this point last year. Last year in March there was a big jump in dividend income that was not repeated this year. Part of this was due to two positions switching when they made their dividend payments. However, looking at the February, March and April months, 2018 saw more dividends that 2017 and the same applies to the March, April and May time frame. February saw a 64% YoY increase and April saw a YoY increase just shy of 70%, which more than made up for the decline in March payments.
Based on currently declared dividends and current share counts, over the next 12 months I can expect $28,124 in dividend payments. This is up a little over $300 from last month's projection. Between the dividends so far collected being 23% more than what I had collected last year, and that $28,124 NTM dividend projection, I am on track to make or exceed my goal of $27,045 in dividend payments for 2018.
I am on track or even slightly ahead of hitting my goals of $27,045 in dividend payments for 2018 having collected just under 40% of that amount already (with just over 40% of the year having passed). The way the universe works, I fully expect one or more of my positions will have a dividend cut. I don't know which company that will effect, or I would have sold it already. So far, just one company has frozen its dividend this year, OHI, and that was after it raised it once this year already (it had had the practice of raising the quarterly dividend a penny each quarter).
While I stay ahead of schedule, I will continue to accumulate shares that grow their dividends faster, like AAPL and NEE. Since I have my current requirements met, I will look further down the road.
Since I introduced a benchmark ETF, how did that do?
The portfolio based on SCHD ( SCHD ) increased just over $10,000 during May, while my DGI portfolio had its market value increase by $14,482. I use Portfolio Visualizer to generate the data for the SCHD based portfolio. SCHD didn't pay out any dividends during May and has paid out just over $3000 for the year so far. I am still quite happy with how my DGI portfolio is performing versus the SCHD benchmark fund.
Conclusion In May I picked up some nice bargains. I think CBRL will work very nicely for me. I am happy to have started positions in both NEE and AAPL, although it looks like I may have to give more thought to valuation since AAPL is now above the buy price I originally set. With a bit over $800 in cash, I will likely be able to buy another chunk of NEE shares which will give AAPL some time in which to drop under my buy price. The summer months should be quite slow on the trading front unless some big news disturbs things.
While I tried to be clear as to why I made the trades I did, I am sure I have fallen short in some fashion. If you don't understand why I made a trade or why I thought it was a good one, or even why I still own certain shares, please ask. There are no dumb questions, and if anyone isn't sure on the why of something I am sure it's not just a single person. So don't be shy, you are not likely to be the only one with the question.
Note: I hope you all got something out of this article. I do appreciate the time you took reading it. If you are one of those who follow me here, I appreciate it; if you'd like to include yourself amongst those individuals, please hit the "Follow" button next to my name as well as following other contributors whose work you enjoy.
